title: Create Maximum Number
statement:
The arrays `nums1` and `nums2` each hold the digits of a number, from the most significant digit to the least. Choose exactly `k` digits in total from the two arrays and arrange them into a new `k`-digit number that is as large as possible, then return its digits as an array.

- Any number of the chosen digits (including none) may come from either array, but digits taken from the same array must appear in the result in the same relative order they had in that array.
- Digits from the two arrays may be interleaved freely.
- "As large as possible" means the result array is the greatest when compared digit by digit from the front.
constraints: Neither nums1 nor nums2 has a leading zero
signature: int[] maxNumber(int[] nums1, int[] nums2, int k)
notes:
## Intuition

Trying every choice of digits and every interleaving is hopeless, but the problem splits into three easy pieces. If we decide that `count` digits come from `nums1` and `k - count` from `nums2`, then the best choice from each array alone is its largest subsequence of that length, and the best result is the largest interleaving of those two subsequences. We enumerate every split and keep the best result.

The largest subsequence of a given length comes from a monotonic stack: while we are still allowed to drop digits, a new digit pops smaller digits off the top, because a bigger digit earlier always wins.

## Approach

1. `pickMax(nums, size)`: scan `nums` keeping a stack whose digits never increase, allowing `drop = nums.length - size` pops; keep the first `size` entries and return them as a digit string.
2. `merge(a, b)`: repeatedly take the front digit of whichever remaining part, `a.slice(i)` or `b.slice(j)`, is greater. Because all entries are single digits, string comparison compares the parts digit by digit, and a part that is a prefix of the other counts as smaller, which is exactly the rule we need.
3. For every `count` from `low = max(0, k - n)` to `high = min(k, m)`, build `candidate` and keep it in `best` when it is greater (all candidates have length `k`).
4. Convert `best` back to an array of digits.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums1 = [3,4,6,5]`, `nums2 = [9,1,2,5,8,3]`, `k = 5`, so `count` runs from 0 to 4.

- `count = 0`: `""` and `"92583"` give `"92583"`.
- `count = 1`: `"6"` and `"9583"` give `"96583"`, a new best.
- `count = 2`: `"65"` and `"983"` give `"98653"`, a new best.
- `count = 3`: `"465"` and `"98"` give `"98465"`, smaller.
- `count = 4`: `"3465"` and `"9"` give `"93465"`, smaller.

The answer is `[9,8,6,5,3]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(k · (m + n + k²)) in the worst case: up to k + 1 splits, each with linear stack passes and a merge of k steps whose suffix comparisons cost up to O(k) each (they usually stop at the first different digit).
- Space: O(m + n + k) for the stacks and candidates.

## Pitfalls

- When the front digits are equal, look further ahead: merging `[6,7]` and `[6,0,4]` must take the 6 from `nums1` first, because `"67"` beats `"604"`. Comparing only front digits fails here.
- Bound `count` so neither array is asked for more digits than it has.
- The stack may end up longer than `size` when the digits never rise; trim it. In Java or C, write the suffix comparison as a loop over both arrays.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `stack`, `drop` | digits kept so far and how many more may be discarded |
| `a`, `b` | the two picked subsequences, as digit strings |
| `i`, `j` | next unused positions in `a` and `b` during the merge |
| `count` | how many digits come from `nums1` |
| `candidate` | best number for this split |
| `best` | best number over all splits so far |

narration.2: pickMax returns the largest subsequence of the given size from one array.
narration.4: drop is how many digits we are still allowed to throw away.
narration.5: Scan the digits left to right.
narration.6: A bigger digit replaces smaller ones on top of the stack while we can still drop digits.
narration.7: Discard the smaller digit; the bigger one should come earlier.
narration.10: Keep the current digit for now.
narration.12: Trim any extra digits at the end and turn the picks into a digit string.
narration.18: Merge until both strings are used up.
narration.19: Compare the remaining parts as strings, so equal front digits are settled by the digits after them.
narration.20: a's remaining part is at least as large: take its front digit.
narration.28: best starts empty, so the first candidate always replaces it.
narration.29: nums2 can supply at most n digits, so nums1 must give at least k - n.
narration.30: nums1 cannot give more than k digits or more than it has.
narration.31: Try every way to split the k digits between the two arrays.
narration.32: Best picks from each array, merged into the best k-digit number for this split.
narration.33: Candidates have the same length, so string comparison finds the larger number.
narration.35: Turn the best digit string back into an array of numbers.
